framework_name: DDI & AI Skills and Capabilities Framework
framework_description: Evidence-based frameworks for Digital, Data, Innovation and AI (DDI & AI) upskilling in the UK Civil Service.

levels.name: Novice
levels.definition: Needs direct support to function. Cannot do this independently yet.

levels.name: Awareness
levels.definition: Can do this reliably with light touch guidance available. Doesn't need hand-holding but isn't fully independent.

levels.name: Working
levels.definition: Fully reliable and independent within their own role and context. No support needed for routine situations.

levels.name: Practitioner
levels.definition: The person others turn to informally. A strong, trusted team member who goes beyond their own work to help others.

levels.name: Expert
levels.definition: Sets direction beyond your immediate team. Reached through specialist depth in a domain, or through enabling leadership — shaping culture, commissioning experts and sustaining transversal practice at scale.

transversal_capabilities.name: Systems Thinking
transversal_capabilities.definition: Analyses how digital, data and AI systems affect people, policies and institutions. Questions problems, interprets data critically, spots unintended impacts and chooses options that improve outcomes.

transversal_capabilities.name: Digital Wellbeing
transversal_capabilities.definition: Creates safe, inclusive spaces for colleagues and citizens to engage with digital change. Shows empathy, communicates clearly and models emotionally intelligent behaviours.

transversal_capabilities.name: Ethical Practice
transversal_capabilities.definition: Makes responsible digital and AI decisions that protect rights and build public trust. Anticipates risks, designs around user needs and ensures fairness and safety.

transversal_capabilities.name: Collaborative Working
transversal_capabilities.definition: Brings together diverse perspectives to deliver joined-up digital services. Shares information, co-creates with users and coordinates work for benefits across the whole system.

transversal_capabilities.name: Continuous Learning
transversal_capabilities.definition: Stays curious, experiments with new tools, reflects on outcomes, seeks feedback and refines practices to keep improving performance and service quality.

design_principles: Knowledge rows carry no transversal tags — they describe understanding rather than doing.
Transversal tags carry cross-cutting dimensions so individual rows stay focused on specific, assessable behaviours.
Behaviour rows only exist where the behaviour is genuinely distinctive to that strand.
Practitioner descriptors avoid project-specific language; use 'area of work' or 'team' instead of 'project' to ensure descriptors work for operational as well as project-based roles.

domains.domain_description: Working effectively in a digital workplace — digital tools, accessible digital content, user-centred digital services, leading in a digital age and handling information well. This domain is here because most civil service work is delivered through digital channels and systems. Nearly everyone needs foundational digital confidence, be it using email applications or collaboration tools. Service design, transformation and leadership apply when you shape how teams or services work.

skills.strand_definition: Uses the software, platforms and online tools needed for modern workplace tasks — including communicating, collaborating, managing information and working securely — with confidence and good judgement in any work setting.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using digital tools and software to complete everyday tasks?

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to use simple digital tools for everyday tasks such as logging in, finding basic information or joining an online meeting. Needs help when problems occur but shows curiosity and asks questions to learn.

Uses common digital tools with support to complete basic tasks such as editing a shared document or updating an online task list. Recognises how digital tools help teams stay connected and asks for help when unsure.

Applies digital tools independently to complete routine tasks such as joining online meetings, sharing documents and tracking progress. Applies agreed ways of working and fixes simple issues to keep work running smoothly.

Organises and independently manages work across multiple digital tools and platforms. Sets up shared spaces, keeps information easy to find and models good online practice. Solves most everyday digital issues and supports colleagues.

Leads on identifying how digital tools and platforms should be best used within the team. Designs simple, consistent ways of working online, promotes secure and inclusive use, and drives improvements that make work quicker and clearer.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in managing and organising information and files so they are easy to find, appropriately shared and kept secure?

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to save and find files in shared spaces but needs support to organise information or apply security settings.
Uses basic file management steps with guidance — saves documents in the right place, follows naming conventions and checks sharing permissions before sending.
Keeps information well-organised and easy to find across shared spaces. Applies agreed security and sharing practices consistently and helps colleagues do the same.
Reviews and improves how information is organised and shared across a team. Identifies risks and inconsistencies and puts in place clearer structures or guidance.
Sets standards for how information is managed, organised and secured across teams. Ensures practices are consistent, secure and easy for everyone to follow.

skills.strand_definition: Selects the right tool for the task — from everyday choices about how to share or collaborate on a piece of work, through to contributing to team standards and organisational procurement decisions.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in deciding which tool or method best fits the task at hand?

descriptors.text: Follows instructions about which tool to use for a task but needs support to understand why one option might suit better than another.

Recognises that different tools suit different purposes and asks for guidance when unsure which to use. Begins to make simple choices independently, such as whether to email a document or share it in a collaborative space.

Makes routine tool choices independently and with confidence — selecting the right platform, format or method for the task. Explains choices simply to colleagues and adapts when a chosen tool isn't working well.

Helps teams develop consistent, well-reasoned approaches to tool selection. Contributes to more formal requirements-gathering and advises colleagues on choices that balance user needs, security and organisational standards.

Sets team standards for tool selection and promotes evidence-based, consistent practice. Contributes to procurement and organisational buying decisions, ensuring choices reflect user needs, value for money and long-term fit.

skills.strand_definition: Creates and shares digital content and communications that everyone can use, applying accessibility standards and meeting legal requirements to support clear, user-friendly digital experiences for all.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of accessibility standards and legal requirements for digital content, and what they mean in practice?

descriptors.text: Has little knowledge of accessibility standards or legal requirements but begins to notice when content might be hard for some people to use and shows curiosity about how to improve it.
Understands what accessibility standards are, why they exist and what the key legal requirements mean for everyday content creation.
Understands core accessibility principles and methods, including how standards apply across different content types, formats and platforms.
Has detailed knowledge of accessibility standards and legal requirements, including how they apply across varied tools, platforms and user needs.
Holds authoritative knowledge of accessibility standards, legal frameworks and emerging good practice, and understands their strategic implications for organisations.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in creating and checking digital content so it meets accessibility standards and works for people with different needs?

descriptors.text: Follows clear instructions to create or edit simple digital content. Begins to notice when something might be hard to read or use and asks questions about how to make it easier.
Uses basic accessibility steps with guidance such as adding alt text, using clear headings or checking colour contrast. Seeks help when unsure how to meet accessibility requirements.

Applies accessibility principles in routine work, creating and editing content that meets departmental standards. Uses clear language, structured layouts and accessible formats. Makes simple improvements when issues are found.

Plans and delivers digital content that meets accessibility standards across different tools and platforms. Considers varied user needs, devices and assistive technologies when designing or reviewing content.

Leads accessible digital practice within individual teams. Sets and maintains best-practice efforts including training, ensures all content meets legal requirements, and reviews major projects for compliance and quality.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in supporting good accessibility practice beyond your own work — whether by modelling it, helping colleagues or flagging where standards aren't being met?

descriptors.text: Begins to notice when colleagues produce content that might not work for everyone and asks questions about how to raise it.
Raises observations about accessibility in team discussions and shares simple tips or guidance with colleagues when opportunities arise.
Actively supports colleagues to meet accessibility standards. Shares examples of good practice, flags issues constructively and helps others understand why accessibility matters.

Leads on embedding accessible content practice across projects. Coaches colleagues, reviews others' work for accessibility and makes the case for prioritising it when it is deprioritised under delivery pressure.
Promotes a culture where accessibility is a default expectation. Ensures it is built into training, ways of working and major decisions, and holds teams accountable for meeting legal standards.

skills.strand_definition: Ensures the information you work with is accurate, current and well-managed — knowing where it came from, keeping it appropriately organised and protected, and disposing of it correctly when it is no longer needed.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in checking that the information you work with and share is accurate, current and from a reliable source?
rows.source_note: Grounded in GovS 002 (version control, provenance, currency) and established information management practice.

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to check simple information such as confirming where it came from or when it was last updated. Begins to notice when something looks wrong or out of date and asks for help to correct it.

Uses basic checks to confirm that information is accurate and current, such as checking the source, looking for a version number or asking whether guidance has been updated. Recognises when information looks unreliable and reports it to others.

Applies routine checks to keep information accurate and trustworthy. Verifies sources, identifies the authoritative version, corrects errors within their area of work and flags issues when information looks inconsistent or out of date.

Reviews how information is sourced, verified and maintained across projects. Identifies patterns of inaccuracy or unreliability, makes improvements and coaches colleagues to apply consistent checks. Ensures information used in decisions is traceable and well evidenced.

Sets standards for how information accuracy and reliability are maintained across teams. Ensures version control, provenance and currency are built into ways of working. Reviews major work to confirm information is well governed and promotes a culture of critical, evidence-based information use.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in organising, classifying and managing information and files so they are easy to find, appropriately protected and correctly disposed of when no longer needed?
rows.source_note: Grounded in GovS 002 (classification, provenance, disposal, version control).

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to save files in the right place and begins to notice why organising information carefully matters. Needs support to understand classification or access settings.

Saves documents in agreed locations, follows basic naming conventions and applies simple access or security settings with guidance. Understands that different information needs different levels of protection and asks for help when unsure.

Organises and maintains files and shared spaces so information is easy to find and consistently structured. Applies correct classification and access controls, follows agreed retention and disposal processes and helps colleagues do the same.

Reviews and improves how information is organised, classified and managed across projects. Identifies risks such as incorrect classification, oversharing or information being retained longer than necessary. Coaches colleagues and ensures practices meet organisational standards.

Sets standards for how information is organised, classified, protected and disposed of across teams. Ensures classification, access control and retention policies are practical, consistently applied and built into team ways of working. Reviews major work to confirm information is well governed throughout its lifecycle.

skills.strand_definition: Understands the needs of the people your work affects and uses that understanding to improve how services and processes are designed and delivered.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of user-centred principles and why understanding user needs matters for the work you do?

descriptors.text: Has little knowledge of user-centred principles but begins to notice when something is hard to use and shows curiosity about why that matters.
Understands the basic idea that services should be designed around the needs of the people who use them, and can explain why this leads to better outcomes.
Understands core user-centred principles and methods, including how research and testing feed into design and delivery decisions.
Has detailed understanding of user-centred practice, including how to apply it across complex or multi-team projects and how to make the case for it to others.
Holds authoritative knowledge of user-centred principles and their strategic value, including how they connect to policy, delivery and public trust.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in finding out what users need — and using that insight to improve your work or processes?

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to help gather simple feedback or observations but needs support to understand what to do with them.
Helps collect feedback and takes part in simple research or testing activities. Shares observations with colleagues and recognises patterns in what users find difficult.
Applies straightforward methods to gather and interpret user feedback. Shares insights with design or delivery colleagues and contributes to decisions about how to improve services.
Plans and runs research and testing activities, ensuring findings inform design and delivery. Coaches colleagues to apply user-centred methods consistently across projects.
Ensures research, testing and feedback are embedded in design and delivery processes across teams. Works with leaders to sustain a culture of continuous improvement in user experience.

rows.question: How would you rate your ability to keep user needs in view when other priorities or pressures are pulling in a different direction?
rows.source_note: Amber — drawn from DDAT specialist framework for user researchers. Open question for client: is this expectation appropriate for non-specialist civil servants?

descriptors.text: Begins to notice when something doesn't seem to work well for users and asks questions about why decisions were made that way.
Raises observations about user needs in team discussions and supports colleagues in considering the impact of decisions on users.
Speaks up when user needs risk being overlooked in delivery decisions. Uses evidence from research or feedback to support their point of view.
Actively challenges decisions that deprioritise user needs and helps teams find ways to balance delivery pressures with user outcomes.
Models and promotes a culture where user needs are treated as non-negotiable. Supports leaders to make decisions that maintain public trust and service quality under pressure.

skills.strand_name: Making digital services work for everyone
skills.strand_definition: Ensures digital public services work for everyone who needs them, reflecting the diverse needs, backgrounds and circumstances of all users and applying government guidance on inclusive design.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of what inclusive design means for digital work and services, and what government guidance says about designing for everyone?

descriptors.text: Has little knowledge of inclusive design principles but begins to notice when something might not work for certain users and asks questions about how to make it fairer.
Understands what inclusive design means and why it matters — that services should work for everyone, including people who face barriers due to circumstances, disability, language or confidence.
Understands core inclusive design principles and how government guidance applies them in practice, including what makes services hard to access for some people.
Has detailed knowledge of inclusive design requirements, including legal duties, good practice guidance and how to apply them across complex or multi-team work.
Holds authoritative knowledge of inclusive design principles, legal frameworks and emerging practice; understands their strategic implications for public service delivery.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in finding out about the different needs, backgrounds and circumstances of the people your work affects?

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to help create or test content for different users but needs support to understand what makes something inclusive or exclusive.
Uses basic inclusive design steps with guidance, such as checking that language, images or layouts work for different users. Identifies simple ways to make things clearer or more welcoming.

Applies inclusive design principles in routine work; engages with different user groups, adapts approaches based on feedback and uses government guidance to make services easier to use for people with varied backgrounds and needs.

Plans and runs user research and engagement that includes people with varied backgrounds and experiences. Reviews services to check they reflect diverse user needs and leads on adopting inclusive design principles across work.

Sets the direction for inclusive digital design across teams. Ensures inclusivity is built into training and ways of working, and reviews major work to confirm it reflects the needs of all users — including those hardest to reach.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using what you learn about users to shape or change your work?

descriptors.text: Does not yet adapt work based on user feedback independently. Follows instructions to make suggested changes.
Makes small changes to content or processes based on feedback or observations about what users find difficult.
Applies what is learned from users to improve work. Tests changes, checks whether they help and iterates based on further feedback.
Leads improvement work based on user insight across a team; ensures changes are tested, evaluated and embedded.
Shapes how user insight drives continuous improvement across teams; ensures learning from diverse users is built into how services evolve.

rows.question: How would you rate your ability to ensure the needs of people who are harder to reach or more likely to be excluded are considered in your work from the start?

descriptors.text: Begins to notice when something might not work for certain users and asks questions about how to make it fairer or easier to use.
Raises concerns when something seems likely to exclude certain users and looks for ways to make it more welcoming.
Consistently applies an inclusive mindset in everyday work — questioning assumptions, sharing examples of good practice and encouraging others to consider who might be left out.

Leads by example on inclusive practice. Coaches colleagues to consider diverse user needs from the start and challenges approaches that risk excluding people. Reviews work to identify and address gaps.

Promotes a culture where inclusive thinking is a default expectation. Sets the standard for how teams consider excluded and harder-to-reach users and ensures this is built into training, ways of working and major decisions.

skills.strand_definition: Shapes how your team uses technology to work better and deliver more — championing digital, data and AI approaches, managing change confidently and building the capability and confidence of others.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of how digital, data and AI can transform the way teams work and deliver outcomes?

descriptors.text: Has little knowledge of how digital, data and AI can change the way teams work, but notices when technology makes tasks easier or faster and shows curiosity about how transformation happens.
Understands that digital, data and AI can make work more efficient, fair and effective, and can describe in simple terms how technology has improved services or ways of working.
Understands how digital, data and AI approaches can be applied to improve everyday work and service delivery, including common opportunities and barriers to adoption.
Has detailed knowledge of how to plan and deliver technology-enabled change, including how to balance innovation, risk, efficiency and public value.

Holds authoritative understanding of how digital, data and AI transformation works at a strategic level, including how to build long-term capability and align technology adoption with organisational priorities.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in encouraging and supporting colleagues to adopt digital, data and AI approaches in your work?

descriptors.text: Follows instructions to use digital tools and systems that support change, and begins to notice opportunities where technology could improve outcomes.
Uses digital tools in own work and shares ideas for small improvements. Recognises how technology can make work more efficient and seeks guidance on how to contribute to adoption.

Applies digital, data and AI approaches to improve everyday work and contributes ideas for innovation. Helps colleagues try new tools responsibly and shares examples of how technology improves outcomes.
Plans and delivers technology-enabled change that balances innovation, efficiency and public value. Leads adoption initiatives, coaches colleagues and builds team confidence in new ways of working.

Sets the vision for digital, data and AI adoption across teams. Ensures technology-enabled change drives efficiency and aligns with organisational priorities, building long-term capability and confidence.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in helping colleagues feel confident about digital change — including when they are uncertain or sceptical?
rows.source_note: Cross-domain flag: when writing Innovation domain, check this B1 against psychological safety and culture of permission content — distinct but related territory.

descriptors.text: Begins to notice when colleagues feel uncertain about new technology and asks questions about how to help them feel more confident.
Recognises that people respond differently to digital change and supports colleagues by sharing simple, positive examples of technology improving work.
Addresses concerns about new technology openly and honestly. Shares evidence of benefits and helps colleagues build confidence through practical experience and peer support.
Actively manages resistance to digital change by understanding its causes and adapting approaches to build trust. Creates opportunities for colleagues to develop confidence in new ways of working.

Models and promotes a culture where digital change is approached with curiosity and confidence. Ensures teams feel supported through transformation and that trust is built and maintained at every stage.

domains.domain_description: Working responsibly with data — from everyday literacy and quality through analysis, evidence-based decisions and sharing. This domain is here because almost every role uses data somehow, even if you are not a data specialist foundational skills apply widely. Deeper quality, analysis and sharing expectations rise when data is central to your work or at higher grades.

skills.strand_definition: Builds the foundational understanding, skills and behaviours needed to work confidently and responsibly with data, recognising that evidence-based decisions lead to better outcomes.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of data and its role in decision-making?

descriptors.text: Basic or minimal knowledge of what data is or how it supports decisions.
Understands what data is, how it is created and stored, and why evidence-based decisions lead to better outcomes.
Confidently understands core data concepts and how data flows through systems to support decisions.
Deep understanding of data as a tool to support decision-making.
Authoritative knowledge of data concepts and strategy; shapes data knowledge across teams.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using data in your day-to-day work?

descriptors.text: Finds and retrieves simple data with direct support, such as locating a record or looking up a figure.
Uses basic data independently to complete simple tasks such as updating a record or checking totals.
Uses data confidently and consistently in routine work; compares figures, checks accuracy and applies agreed ways of working.
Manages data across multiple tools; sets up shared spaces, models good practice and supports colleagues.
Leads how data is used across teams; designs consistent ways of working and drives improvements.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using the data tools and systems relevant to your role?

descriptors.text: Has little or no experience using data tools. Needs step-by-step instruction for the simplest tasks.
Can follow instructions to complete basic tasks in familiar tools, such as opening a report or entering a value.
Uses standard tools and systems independently to complete routine tasks such as updating records, running reports or checking totals.
Works confidently across multiple tools and systems, combining data sources and adapting to new tools with limited support.
Masters a wide range of tools and evaluates new ones. Advises others on the best tools for a given purpose.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in drawing on data rather than instinct or assumption when you need to make a decision?

descriptors.text: Does not yet use data to inform decisions independently. Follows instructions to find or check figures.
Uses simple data to help make basic decisions, such as checking a figure before sending a report.
Applies data regularly to support decisions in own work; draws straightforward conclusions and shares findings clearly.
Uses data to make well-reasoned recommendations and challenge assumptions; helps teams make evidence-based decisions.
Shapes how data informs decisions at a strategic level; champions evidence-based thinking and builds capability across teams.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in making sure the data you work with and share is handled safely and responsibly?

descriptors.text: Not yet aware of responsibilities around data handling. May make mistakes without realising the risk.
Understands that data must be handled carefully and follows basic rules when reminded.
Consistently follows data handling rules, protects sensitive information and raises concerns when something seems wrong.
Models careful and responsible data use, proactively identifies risks and ensures the team follows secure practices.
Champions responsible data use at a strategic level, leads on compliance and embeds a culture of data ethics.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in evaluating and improving the data processes you work with?

descriptors.text: Does not yet evaluate data processes. Works within whatever is in place.
Notices when something could work better and mentions it, even if not yet taking action.
Takes steps to improve own data practices, applies lessons learned and shares what works with the team.
Identifies systemic issues and drives practical improvements, working with others to raise standards across the team.
Sets the strategic direction for data improvement, influences policy and governance and leads change that has lasting impact.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in questioning the data you use — for example, where it came from, how it was collected, or whether it tells the full story?

descriptors.text: Accepts data at face value. Does not yet question sources, methods or representativeness.
Begins to ask basic questions about data — where it came from, whether it looks right — when prompted.
Routinely checks data for obvious issues such as missing values, outliers or inconsistencies before using it.
Critically evaluates data quality, bias and limitations; challenges poor data use and helps colleagues develop similar habits.
Shapes a culture of critical data evaluation across teams; sets standards for what counts as reliable evidence.

skills.strand_definition: Reads charts, graphs and other visual representations of data to extract meaning, identify patterns and support clear communication of evidence.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of visual data — including how charts and tables work, and how visual formats can help or mislead?

descriptors.text: Little knowledge of what visual data is or why it is used. May not yet know how to read a chart independently.
Understands that charts and graphs present data visually to make patterns easier to spot and communicate.
Understands a range of common chart types, when to use them and how to read them accurately.
Understands how design choices in visualisations can help or hinder accurate interpretation; knows when visuals can mislead.
Authoritative knowledge of data visualisation principles; shapes how data is presented to ensure clarity, accuracy and accessibility.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in reading and extracting meaning from charts and tables?

descriptors.text: Can identify basic features of a chart such as a title or axis label but needs support to understand what the data shows.
Reads simple charts and tables with guidance; identifies key figures and basic trends.
Reads and interprets a range of charts and tables independently; spots patterns, checks accuracy and draws relevant conclusions.
Interprets complex or unfamiliar visualisations confidently; identifies limitations, questions assumptions and draws nuanced insights.
Analyses and evaluates visualisations critically; identifies when data is being misrepresented and advises on better approaches.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in creating clear and effective visualisations?

descriptors.text: Does not yet create visualisations independently. Needs guidance to produce even simple charts.
Creates basic charts using standard tools when shown what to do; follows templates or examples.
Produces clear, appropriately labelled visualisations that communicate the main finding to the intended audience.
Designs visualisations that are accurate, accessible and tailored to the audience; advises colleagues on how to present data clearly.
Sets standards for how data is visualised across teams; ensures visualisations are clear, accurate and accessible for all audiences.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in considering whether the visual data you create or share works for people with different needs, including those using assistive technologies?

descriptors.text: Not yet aware that visual data may be inaccessible to some people. Does not consider this when reading or creating charts.
Understands that some people find certain visual formats difficult to use; begins to consider this when creating simple charts.
Checks that visualisations are accessible — for example, not relying on colour alone — and considers whether the format works for all likely users.
Ensures accessibility and inclusion are built into how data is visualised across a team; reviews others' work and raises issues constructively.
Champions accessible and inclusive data visualisation; sets standards and ensures all visual outputs across teams meet accessibility requirements.

skills.strand_definition: Handles data responsibly through each stage of its lifecycle — from collection and storage through to sharing, retention and disposal — following good practice to keep data secure, accurate and useful.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of how data moves through its lifecycle from collection to disposal — including what happens at each stage and why responsible handling throughout matters?

descriptors.text: Little knowledge of data lifecycle stages. May not be aware that data has a lifecycle at all.
Understands that data has a lifecycle — it is collected, stored, used and eventually disposed of — and that each stage has responsibilities.
Understands the key stages of the data lifecycle and the good practice principles that apply at each stage.
Understands how data lifecycle management affects data quality, security and compliance across a team or system.
Authoritative knowledge of data lifecycle management; shapes policy and practice to ensure data is handled responsibly at every stage.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in collecting and recording data correctly?

descriptors.text: Collects or records data with direct support, following step-by-step instructions.
Follows agreed procedures to collect and record data correctly, such as using the right format or completing required fields.
Collects and records data consistently and accurately; follows standards and flags issues when data doesn't look right.
Reviews and improves data collection processes; ensures data is recorded consistently and to a high standard across a team.
Designs data collection processes that are accurate, efficient and compliant; sets standards across teams.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in storing and sharing data securely?

descriptors.text: Needs support to store or share data securely. May not be aware of the risks of unsecured storage or sharing.
Follows basic rules for storing and sharing data — such as using approved systems and not sharing sensitive data without permission.
Stores and shares data securely and consistently, following agreed protocols and checking permissions before sharing.
Reviews how data is stored and shared across a team; identifies risks and puts improvements in place.
Sets standards for secure data storage and sharing across teams; ensures policies are practical, compliant and well understood.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in disposing of data correctly?

descriptors.text: Not yet aware of data disposal requirements. Does not yet act on them independently.
Understands that data must be disposed of correctly and follows instructions to delete or archive data when told to.
Disposes of data correctly and on time, following retention schedules and disposal procedures.
Ensures data disposal is managed consistently across a team; reviews retention schedules and addresses backlogs.
Sets and oversees data disposal standards; ensures retention policies are legally compliant and consistently applied.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in making sure data is handled consistently and responsibly when it crosses team or organisational boundaries?

descriptors.text: Handles data in isolation. Not yet aware of how own data handling connects to or affects other teams.
Begins to understand that data handling decisions can affect other teams; raises questions when unsure how own actions fit into the wider picture.
Considers how own data handling connects to other teams' work; flags issues that could affect shared data and follows up to resolve them.
Actively coordinates data handling across teams; ensures consistency, resolves cross-team issues and builds shared understanding of responsibilities.
Shapes how data handling is coordinated across the organisation; builds systems and relationships that ensure data flows reliably and responsibly between teams.

skills.strand_definition: Reviews and improves data to ensure they are accurate, representative and fit for purpose, helping teams to make reliable decisions and maintain trust in information.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of data quality and why it matters for decisions and outcomes?

descriptors.text: Has no working knowledge of data quality. Begins to notice that some data seem more reliable than others and asks questions about why that matters.

Understands that data quality affects how reliable decisions and services are. Knows that quality can be assessed across dimensions such as accuracy, completeness and consistency, and can explain in simple terms why poor quality data causes problems.

Has sound knowledge of data quality principles and dimensions, and understands that quality is about fitness for purpose — whether data is good enough for the decision or task at hand. Familiar with government guidance on data quality and how it applies in their context.

Has detailed knowledge of data quality including how it interacts with the data lifecycle. Understands how quality issues compound across systems and teams, and knows that communicating quality transparently to the people using data is as important as improving it.

Has authoritative knowledge of data quality principles, dimensions and practices. Understands the importance of treating root causes rather than symptoms, anticipating how changes to systems or processes will affect quality, and driving a culture of continuous improvement at an organisational level.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in identifying, correcting and cleaning data to ensure it is accurate and complete?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet identify or correct data errors independently. With support, begins to notice when something looks wrong, such as a missing entry or an obviously incorrect figure.

Identifies common errors in simple datasets with guidance, such as duplicates, missing values or figures that don't add up. Makes straightforward corrections when shown how, and reports issues that are beyond their ability to fix independently.

Applies routine checks to identify errors, inaccuracies and gaps in data within their area of work. Corrects and cleans data following agreed processes, documents what was changed and why, and escalates issues that require more specialist attention.

Reviews data systematically across a project or team, identifying patterns of error rather than isolated problems. Leads data cleaning activities, distinguishes between surface errors and deeper quality issues, and helps colleagues develop their ability to spot and correct problems.

Sets standards for how data errors are identified, corrected and documented across teams. Ensures checking and cleaning are built into processes rather than bolted on afterwards, and promotes a culture where quality problems are surfaced and treated at source.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in assessing whether data are representative and unbiased?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet assess representativeness or bias independently. Begins to understand that data does not always reflect the full picture and asks questions about who or what might be missing.

Understands that data can be incomplete or skewed in ways that affect decisions. With guidance, begins to ask basic questions about where data came from, who collected it and whether important groups might be missing or underrepresented.

Applies straightforward checks to assess whether data are representative and free from obvious bias. Recognises that the choice of summary measure matters — for example, that a mean can mislead when data are skewed — and flags concerns about how data are being interpreted or used.

Systematically reviews data for representativeness and bias across projects, using evidence to challenge assumptions about what the data shows. Considers whether data collection and sampling methods are sufficient for the conclusions being drawn, and helps colleagues avoid common statistical pitfalls.

Sets standards for how representativeness and bias are assessed across teams. Ensures that data collection and management processes actively account for potential bias, and promotes a culture where the limitations of data are honestly acknowledged and communicated.

skills.strand_definition: Collects, uses and shares data fairly, securely and in line with laws and ethical principles, recognising that legal compliance is the minimum standard and that ethical obligations go further.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of the legal and ethical framework governing how data should be collected, used and shared?

descriptors.text: Has no working knowledge of data law or ethics. Begins to understand that there are rules governing how data can be used and that breaking them can harm people and organisations.

Understands that data use is governed by law and ethical principles, and is aware of key legislation such as data protection law. Knows in simple terms what this means for everyday work — for example, that personal data must be kept secure and only shared appropriately.

Has sound working knowledge of the legal and ethical framework governing data use, including data protection legislation and relevant government guidance. Understands that acting lawfully is the minimum requirement, not the standard to aim for, and knows when to seek advice from specialists such as data protection officers.

Has detailed knowledge of the legal and ethical framework, including how different pieces of legislation interact and how ethical principles apply in complex or ambiguous situations. Recognises that something can be legal but still ethically wrong, and can help colleagues navigate that distinction.

Has authoritative knowledge of the legal and ethical framework governing data use across government. Understands how legislation, policy and ethical standards interact at a strategic level, and actively promotes a culture where ethical data use goes beyond mere compliance.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in checking that data you access, use or share is handled lawfully and ethically?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet make independent judgements about whether data can be accessed, used or shared appropriately. With support, follows clear instructions to handle data safely, such as using secure storage or not sharing files without permission.

Follows established guidance when accessing, using and sharing data. Checks before sharing personal or sensitive data, uses approved channels and asks for help when unsure whether something is appropriate.

Applies legal and ethical requirements confidently in everyday work when accessing, using and sharing data. Uses established tools and processes — such as data sharing agreements or impact assessments — to check that data use is appropriate, and raises concerns when something doesn't feel right.

Reviews how data is being accessed, used and shared across a project or team, applying appropriate tools and frameworks to assure both compliance and ethical standards. Identifies gaps or inconsistencies, helps colleagues navigate less straightforward situations and ensures practice goes beyond legal minimum.

Sets standards for lawful and ethical data access, use and sharing across teams. Ensures that established assurance tools and frameworks are used consistently, that legal compliance is treated as a baseline rather than a destination, and builds a culture where ethical considerations are part of every decision involving data.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in identifying and responding to legal and ethical risks or violations in how data is used?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet identify data risks or violations independently. With support, begins to recognise situations where something might have gone wrong, such as data being shared with the wrong person, and knows to tell someone.

Recognises common data risks and violations with guidance, such as unauthorised sharing or use of data for an unintended purpose. Knows who to report concerns to and follows clear steps when something goes wrong.

Identifies legal and ethical risks in everyday data use and responds appropriately — escalating violations, following incident procedures and helping to limit any harm caused. Understands the difference between a legal breach and an ethical concern that falls short of breaking the law.

Reviews data use across a project or team to proactively identify legal and ethical risks before they become violations. Leads the response when problems occur, ensures lessons are learned and helps colleagues develop their ability to spot and respond to risks.

Sets standards for how legal and ethical risks are identified, assessed and responded to across teams. Ensures that risk identification is proactive rather than reactive, and promotes a culture where concerns are raised early and violations are treated as opportunities to improve rather than just incidents to manage.

skills.strand_definition: Uses agreed rules and formats to keep data consistent and interoperable, supporting effective data use, openness and collaboration across the Civil Service.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of data standards and why consistency and interoperability matter across government?

descriptors.text: Has no working knowledge of data standards. Begins to understand that data needs to be consistent to be useful and asks questions about why agreed rules and formats matter.

Understands that data standards are agreed rules and formats that make data consistent and easier to share across teams and systems. Knows in simple terms why inconsistent data causes problems — for example, that different date formats or naming conventions make data difficult to combine or compare.

Has sound working knowledge of data standards and why they matter for consistency and interoperability across government. Understands how applying standards in their own work contributes to data being usable beyond their immediate team or system.

Has detailed knowledge of data standards including how they interact with data sharing and open data requirements. Understands how standards enable systems to exchange data automatically and can make the case for consistent adoption to colleagues and stakeholders.

Has authoritative knowledge of data standards frameworks and their strategic importance for interoperability across government. Understands how schemas, APIs and related technical standards connect to wider data infrastructure and policy goals, and can guide teams through complex decisions about standards adoption and development.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in applying agreed data standards in your own work and flagging when data doesn't meet them?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet apply data standards independently. With support, begins to follow simple rules for recording information, such as entering dates in a required format or using an approved list of categories.

Follows agreed rules for recording and submitting information, such as using required formats, approved codes or consistent naming conventions. Recognises that doing this makes data easier to use and compare across teams, and asks for help when unsure which format or category to use.

Applies agreed rules and formats consistently and independently when recording, submitting or sharing data. Checks own data before sharing, corrects simple inconsistencies and flags issues that require more specialist attention.

Applies data standards confidently across varied situations and checks that data meets agreed standards across a project or team. Spots and addresses inconsistencies, helps colleagues understand why standards matter and supports more consistent adoption. Contributes to decisions about how standards should be applied or updated in their context, including in relation to open data requirements.

Sets and maintains data standards across teams, ensuring consistent adoption and identifying where existing standards need updating or where new ones are needed. Provides guidance and training, engages with cross-government standards work including open data requirements, and ensures teams understand how their data connects to wider government data infrastructure.

skills.strand_definition: Uses data and analytical tools and techniques to find patterns, draw insights and support evidence-based decisions that improve outcomes.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of data analysis and how it supports decision-making — including what kinds of questions it can answer and what its limitations are?

descriptors.text: Has minimal knowledge of data analysis but begins to understand that examining data carefully leads to better decisions. Recognises simple analytical outputs such as totals or averages with support.

Understands that data analysis involves examining information to find patterns, differences or trends that support decisions. Knows that different analytical approaches suit different questions and that outputs need to be checked for accuracy.

Has sound knowledge of core analytical concepts and methods. Understands how analysis connects to decision-making, including the importance of checking assumptions and being honest about what the data does and does not show.

Has detailed knowledge of analytical methods and tools, including when to use different approaches and when to involve specialist analytical colleagues. Understands the implications of analytical choices for the quality and reliability of conclusions.

Has authoritative knowledge of data analysis including advanced methods, the analytical landscape across government and the strategic value of robust analysis for policy and service delivery. Shapes how analytical capability is understood and built across teams.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using analytical tools and software to work with data?

descriptors.text: Uses simple tools such as spreadsheets with direct support to review small amounts of data; follows step-by-step guidance.
Uses basic analytical tools reliably with light support; sorts, filters and compares data to identify simple patterns and differences.
Uses analytical tools confidently and independently, including spreadsheet features such as pivot tables and charts; checks outputs for accuracy and knows when results look wrong.

Recognises when more advanced tools — such as data visualisation software or statistical packages — would better serve the analysis; can use or commission them and coaches colleagues on tool choice and use.
Understands the landscape of analytical tools including automated and machine learning approaches; guides decisions about when and how to use them and sets standards for tool use across teams.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in working out what question you need to answer and finding the right data to answer it?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet identify independently what data would help answer a question. With support, begins to understand what is being asked and why.
Identifies what data might help answer a simple question with guidance, such as what needs to be compared or measured. Asks for help when unsure whether the right data are available or suitable.
Works out what question needs answering and identifies appropriate data to answer it. Checks that data are relevant, sufficient and suitable before beginning analysis.

Breaks complex or ambiguous questions into manageable parts and identifies the data needed at each stage. Helps colleagues sharpen their questions and challenges assumptions about what data will and won't show.
Shapes how questions are framed across teams, ensuring analysis starts from a clear question rather than available data. Sets standards for how data needs are scoped and documented.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in communicating analytical findings, including uncertainty and limitations?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet communicate analytical findings independently. With support, begins to describe what data show in simple terms.
Shares simple findings with guidance, such as summarising a key figure or trend. Begins to recognise that findings have limitations and flags uncertainty when prompted.
Communicates findings clearly to colleagues, explaining what the data show and what they don't. Acknowledges limitations and uncertainty honestly rather than overstating what the analysis proves.
Presents findings to varied audiences, adapting language and format to suit the context. Clearly articulates confidence levels, caveats and the implications of analytical limitations for decisions.

Sets standards for how analytical findings are communicated across teams, ensuring uncertainty and limitations are consistently and honestly reported. Builds a culture where caveats strengthen rather than undermine analytical credibility.

skills.strand_definition: Works with other teams and organisations to share and reuse data safely and ethically, helping to create collaborative insight, efficiency and improvement.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of data sharing across teams and organisations, including what enables it and what governs it?

descriptors.text: Has no working knowledge of data sharing across teams. Begins to understand that data can be shared beyond their immediate team and asks questions about what makes that possible and what the rules are.

Understands that data sharing across teams and organisations is governed by rules and agreements, and that it requires both technical and legal conditions to be met. Knows in simple terms why sharing data can improve outcomes and why those rules exist to protect people and organisations.

Has sound working knowledge of what enables and governs data sharing across teams and organisations, including relevant legal frameworks, data sharing agreements and good practice guidance. Understands that both over-caution and careless sharing can cause harm, and knows when to seek advice.

Has detailed knowledge of the legal, technical and organisational conditions that enable effective data sharing. Understands how data sharing agreements, access controls and governance frameworks work in practice, and can identify and address barriers that prevent teams from sharing data effectively and responsibly.

Has authoritative knowledge of data sharing frameworks, standards and governance across government. Understands how legal, technical and cultural factors interact to enable or block data sharing, and can guide teams and organisations through complex or sensitive data sharing decisions.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in sharing data with other teams and organisations safely, lawfully and effectively?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet share data with other teams independently. With support, follows clear instructions to share approved files or information using agreed channels.

Shares data with other teams using approved channels and following established guidance. Begins to understand that how data is shared matters as well as whether it is shared — for example, that a spreadsheet is more useful to recipients than a screenshot. Asks for help when unsure about permissions or formats.

Shares data with other teams and organisations safely and lawfully, following agreed processes and using appropriate tools and agreements. Chooses formats that recipients can actually work with rather than just formats that are convenient to send, and raises concerns when requests feel unclear or inappropriate.

Leads data sharing activities across projects, ensuring the right legal, technical and governance conditions are met. Helps colleagues navigate sharing requests confidently, addresses barriers that prevent legitimate sharing and ensures data is shared in formats that colleagues and partners can readily work with.

Sets standards for how data is shared across teams and organisations, ensuring processes are safe, lawful and as frictionless as possible. Identifies systemic barriers to sharing and works across organisational boundaries to remove them, promoting a culture where responsible sharing in useful, reusable formats is the default rather than the exception.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in finding, accessing and reusing data that others have shared?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet find or access shared data independently. With support, begins to understand that data collected by others may already exist and could be useful for their work.

Finds and accesses shared data using approved channels and following established guidance. Begins to think about what data might already exist before collecting new data, and asks colleagues who might hold relevant information.

Finds, accesses and reuses data that others have shared, checking that use is lawful and appropriate. Proactively considers what data might help answer a question and who across their organisation might already hold it, rather than defaulting to collecting new data.

Identifies opportunities to reuse data across projects, thinking creatively about which teams or organisations might hold relevant data and brokering connections to make it accessible. Helps colleagues develop the habit of looking for existing data before collecting new data.

Promotes a culture where finding and reusing shared data is the default starting point. Works creatively across organisational boundaries to surface data that teams didn't know existed, reduces duplication across government and makes data more findable and accessible for others.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in working with others to make data sharing across your organisation easier and more consistent?

descriptors.text: Begins to notice when data sharing between teams is slow or blocked and asks questions about why. Follows clear instructions to support simple data sharing tasks.

Understands that effective data sharing depends on relationships and trust as much as rules and processes. Begins to build connections with colleagues in other teams and asks questions about what data they hold and how it might be shared.

Actively builds working relationships that make data sharing easier and more effective. Approaches data sharing requests with an enabling mindset, looking for ways to share responsibly rather than reasons to refuse, and encourages colleagues to do the same.

Builds and maintains relationships across teams and organisations that enable regular, effective data sharing. Challenges a culture of unnecessary caution or restriction, helps colleagues develop confidence in sharing responsibly and models an enabling approach in their own practice.

Shapes the culture around data sharing across teams and organisations, making responsible openness the default rather than the exception. Builds networks and partnerships that unlock data sharing at scale, and champions the value of collaborative data use for improving outcomes and public value.

domains.domain_description: How people and teams improve how work is done — creating conditions for ideas, understanding problems, testing approaches and making change stick. This domain is here because adaptation and improvement are part of public service, not a separate profession. Everyone can show curiosity. Psychological safety, continuous improvement, prototyping and embedding change at scale need wider influence and remit.

skills.strand_definition: Creates the conditions for colleagues to share ideas, try new approaches and learn from failure, building a team environment where experimentation and honest reflection are normal.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of how people respond to uncertainty and change at work, and why that affects whether innovation happens?

descriptors.text: Has no formal knowledge of how people respond to uncertainty and change. Begins to notice that some people and teams seem more comfortable with risk and new ideas than others, and is curious about what makes that difference.

Understands that people's responses to change and uncertainty are shaped by their environment as much as their personality — and that fear of judgement, blame or instability can stop good ideas from surfacing. Recognises that this applies to themselves as well as others.

Understands the psychological and organisational mechanisms that shape how people respond to change and risk — including why people resist new ideas, how change affects motivation and confidence, and what conditions make experimentation feel safe. Can connect this understanding to what they observe in their own team.

Has detailed knowledge of research and frameworks relating to psychological safety, change management and resilience — including how leadership behaviour, organisational culture and workload affect people's capacity to adapt and innovate. Uses this knowledge to diagnose why a team or environment is or isn't conducive to innovation.

Holds authoritative understanding of the organisational psychology underpinning both psychological safety and adaptability to change. Draws on research and evidence to advise on how to build environments where people can cope with uncertainty and take creative risks sustainably — and understands how these conditions connect to broader organisational culture and innovation capability.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in identifying what it takes to get a new idea off the ground — who needs convincing, what concerns to address, and how to frame the proposal?

descriptors.text: Has no experience building a case for new ideas. Begins to notice that proposals need more than a good idea behind them and asks questions about what makes some cases more persuasive than others.

Understands that getting support for new approaches requires identifying who needs to be involved, what their concerns might be and how to address them. With guidance, begins to think about how to frame a proposal and who the right people to approach might be.

Applies straightforward techniques to build a case for new ideas — identifying key stakeholders, anticipating objections and framing proposals in terms of benefits and manageable risk. Knows how to find a sponsor for a small-scale experiment and how to present evidence clearly to support a proposal.

Applies a systematic approach to making the case for innovation — mapping stakeholders, understanding their priorities and risk concerns, and tailoring proposals accordingly. Coaches colleagues on how to frame ideas persuasively and helps them identify the right routes to seek support.

Has deep knowledge of how organisational decision-making works and what it takes to build lasting support for innovation. Advises others on influencing strategies, helps teams develop strong proposals, and contributes to building organisational processes that make it easier to get new ideas heard and evaluated fairly.

rows.question: How would you rate your effectiveness in making it feel safe for colleagues to share ideas, try new things and admit when things go wrong?

descriptors.text: Has no established practice here. Begins to notice how others respond to new ideas and mistakes, and reflects on how their own reactions might affect whether colleagues feel comfortable speaking up.

Responds openly and constructively when colleagues share ideas or admit mistakes, and avoids reactions that might discourage people from speaking up. Recognises that their own behaviour — however junior their role — contributes to how safe others feel to take creative risks.

Consistently models behaviours that signal it is safe to experiment and fail — responding to unsuccessful attempts with curiosity rather than blame, actively inviting dissenting views and acknowledging their own uncertainties and mistakes. Encourages colleagues to share early-stage ideas before they are fully formed.

Actively works to build a team environment where experimentation is expected and failure is treated as a source of learning rather than a cause for blame. Addresses behaviours that chill creative risk-taking, makes space in team processes for reflection on what didn't work, and helps colleagues reframe unsuccessful experiments constructively.

Shapes team and organisational culture so that psychological safety is a structural feature, not dependent on individual personalities or relationships. Establishes norms, processes and leadership expectations that sustain a culture of honest experimentation, and helps other leaders understand their role in building and protecting it.

rows.question: How would you rate your effectiveness in responding when an experiment or new idea doesn't work out — in your own work and when it happens to colleagues?

descriptors.text: Has little experience of how to respond constructively when things go wrong. Begins to notice their own reactions to failure — in their own work and others' — and reflects on whether those reactions help or hinder learning.

Understands that how people respond to failure shapes whether others feel safe to experiment. Tries to respond to their own mistakes and others' with openness rather than defensiveness, and recognises when a reaction — including their own — might discourage future risk-taking.

Responds to unsuccessful experiments — their own and colleagues' — with curiosity and a focus on learning rather than blame. Asks what can be learned rather than what went wrong, and helps colleagues extract useful insight from things that didn't work out as planned.

Models a consistently constructive response to failure and helps teams develop shared practices for reflecting on and learning from experiments that don't succeed. Recognises the difference between productive failure — where learning occurred — and avoidable failure, and helps teams make that distinction without blame.

Shapes how failure is understood and treated across teams, ensuring that learning from unsuccessful experiments is built into ways of working rather than left to individual goodwill. Helps leaders understand their own role in modelling healthy responses to failure and the long-term cost of cultures where mistakes are hidden.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in coping with change at work and supporting colleagues who are finding it hard?

descriptors.text: Has little experience of managing their own response to significant change at work. Begins to notice how change affects their motivation and ways of working, and asks for support when feeling uncertain or overwhelmed.

Maintains basic effectiveness when facing change, with support. Recognises when change is affecting their own or colleagues' confidence and asks questions about how to adjust. Begins to develop personal strategies for staying productive when processes, tools or priorities shift.

Adapts their own working practices when facing change, maintaining effectiveness without significant loss of productivity. Supports colleagues by sharing what helps them adjust, normalising uncertainty as a feature of innovative environments and encouraging others not to let discomfort with change prevent them from trying new things.

Maintains effectiveness and supports colleagues through sustained or rapid change, helping teams stay productive and psychologically safe even when direction is unclear. Recognises the cumulative toll of continuous change and takes practical steps to protect team wellbeing and capacity to innovate under pressure.

Builds team-wide adaptability as a sustained capability rather than a response to individual change events. Helps leaders understand the relationship between change management, psychological safety and innovation capacity, and ensures teams have the support, structures and culture to keep innovating even in conditions of significant uncertainty.

skills.strand_definition: Spots where innovation is most likely to make a real difference, using evidence and user insight to distinguish genuine opportunities from novelty for its own sake.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of where innovation is most likely to make a real difference — and what makes something a genuine opportunity rather than change for its own sake?

descriptors.text: Has little formal knowledge of what innovation means in a public sector context. Begins to notice when processes feel unnecessarily slow or complicated and is curious about whether things could be done differently.

Understands that innovation means finding better ways to deliver services or outcomes — not just adopting new technology. Recognises that genuine opportunities for improvement often come from user needs, inefficient processes or unmet demands, and that not every problem requires an innovative solution.

Understands how to distinguish genuine innovation opportunities from change for its own sake. Knows that the strongest opportunities tend to cluster around persistent user pain points, processes that haven't kept pace with available technology, and places where evidence consistently points to poor outcomes.

Has detailed understanding of how to assess the landscape for innovation opportunities — including how to read data, user research and organisational context to identify where change would deliver the greatest value. Understands the difference between incremental improvement and step-change innovation, and when each is appropriate.

Holds authoritative understanding of where and how innovation creates sustainable public value — including the systemic conditions that enable or suppress it, how innovation opportunity landscapes shift over time, and how to build organisational knowledge that continuously surfaces high-value opportunities.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using evidence to identify where innovation or improvement is most needed — and assess whether an opportunity is realistic and worth pursuing?

descriptors.text: Has no established practice of identifying or evaluating opportunities for improvement. Begins to notice when something could work better and asks questions about what makes an opportunity worth acting on.

Uses simple evidence sources with guidance — such as feedback, complaints data or observation — to spot where something isn't working well. With guidance, begins to think through whether an opportunity is realistic, considering whether there is a clear problem, whether users would benefit and whether it is broadly achievable.

Applies straightforward methods to identify and assess innovation opportunities. Draws on data, user feedback and process observation to build an evidence-based case for where improvement is needed, and weighs likely impact against feasibility, resource requirements and risk. Presents a clear, honest assessment of whether an opportunity is worth pursuing.

Systematically combines multiple evidence sources to identify high-value opportunities and makes confident, well-reasoned judgments about whether they are worth pursuing. Considers public sector specific constraints — policy alignment, risk appetite, procurement requirements — alongside impact and feasibility. Helps colleagues develop more rigorous approaches to both finding and evaluating opportunities.

Designs and embeds approaches across teams for continuously scanning evidence and evaluating opportunities in a consistent, transparent way. Builds shared criteria for assessing where innovation effort should be focused and advises senior leaders on prioritisation decisions, ensuring the organisation develops a mature, honest approach to identifying and acting on the most valuable opportunities.

rows.question: How would you rate how consistently you think about what users actually experience when deciding where innovation or improvement is most needed?

descriptors.text: Has little habit of thinking about what users actually experience. Begins to notice when services seem designed around internal processes rather than user needs, and asks questions about how that could be different.

Begins to consider what users actually experience when thinking about where things could be improved. Recognises that the most valuable opportunities for innovation often come from genuine user pain points rather than internal priorities, and seeks out simple ways to understand what users find difficult.

Consistently draws on understanding of user experience when identifying where innovation is needed — going beyond what data shows to consider what it feels like to use a service. Brings user perspectives into team discussions about improvement and challenges proposals that aren't grounded in genuine user need.

Habitually anchors innovation thinking in deep understanding of user experience, actively seeking out direct contact with users and ensuring that opportunity identification across projects is driven by what users actually need rather than what is internally convenient. Coaches colleagues to develop the same habit.

Shapes a team culture where user experience is the primary lens through which innovation opportunities are identified and evaluated. Ensures that direct user insight — not just data or assumption — informs decisions about where to focus innovation effort, and challenges organisational tendencies to innovate around internal convenience rather than genuine user need.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in constructively challenging established ways of working when you think something could be done better?

descriptors.text: Notices when processes or ways of working seem unnecessarily complicated or slow, but has little confidence in raising this. Begins to ask questions — at least privately — about why things are done a particular way and whether there might be a better approach.

Asks constructive questions about why things are done a particular way, with support. Recognises that challenging established practices respectfully is a valuable contribution, not a source of disruption, and begins to share observations about processes that could work better.

Constructively challenges established ways of working when there is a good reason to — raising questions, sharing evidence and suggesting alternatives in ways that are honest and respectful. Does not accept 'we've always done it this way' as a sufficient justification, and encourages colleagues to think critically about processes they take for granted.

Actively and consistently challenges assumptions about how work is done, bringing evidence and user insight to bear on why existing approaches may no longer be fit for purpose. Creates space in team discussions for honest questioning of established practice, and helps colleagues develop the confidence and skills to do the same.

Builds a team culture where constructive challenge of the status quo is expected and valued — not tolerated as an exception. Models intellectual honesty about what isn't working, helps leaders understand the cost of unchallenged assumptions, and ensures that questioning established practice is treated as a sign of engagement rather than a source of risk.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in seeking out connections between your work and what's happening elsewhere — in other teams, disciplines or sectors — to inform where and how you innovate?

descriptors.text: Begins to notice connections between their own work and how similar challenges are faced or approached elsewhere — in other teams, services or sectors. Shows curiosity about different contexts and asks questions about what could be learned from them.

Actively looks beyond their immediate team for ideas, approaches and shared challenges that might be relevant to their own work. Spots patterns across different areas — noticing when a problem they're facing resembles something encountered elsewhere — and shares these observations with colleagues.

Deliberately seeks out perspectives from outside their immediate context — other teams, disciplines or sectors — and brings what they learn back into how they identify and frame innovation opportunities. Helps colleagues make connections between their work and ideas from elsewhere, encouraging cross-pollination of thinking.

Builds and maintains relationships across organisational and sectoral boundaries that bring a regular flow of fresh perspectives and ideas into their team. Creates informal and structured opportunities for colleagues to encounter thinking from outside their immediate context, and ensures that cross-boundary insight informs how the team identifies and pursues innovation opportunities.

Cultivates networks, partnerships and team conditions that systematically surface transformative ideas over the long term. Ensures that the organisation maintains meaningful connections with external communities of practice, other sectors and international peers, and builds a culture where curiosity about how others solve problems is a recognised and valued source of innovation opportunity.

skills.strand_definition: Applies the stages of the innovation lifecycle — from identifying a problem through to testing, refining and deciding whether to scale, stop or adapt — with appropriate rigour at each stage.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of the stages of the innovation lifecycle, from identifying a problem through to testing, refining and deciding whether to stop or scale a solution?

descriptors.text: Has little or no practical knowledge of the stages of the innovation lifecycle.
Understands that innovation moves through distinct stages, from problem to solution, and can name them in broad terms.
Understands the stages of the innovation lifecycle and can explain how they apply to their own work.
Has detailed understanding of the lifecycle including why moving between stages in response to evidence matters; helps colleagues in their area of work apply it well.
Holds authoritative knowledge of the lifecycle across contexts; shapes how the lifecycle is taught, applied or governed more widely.
