skills.strand_definition: Tries out ideas on a small scale first, using prototypes, pilots and minimum viable products to learn quickly and reduce risk before committing to larger investment.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of what makes a test or prototype genuinely useful, such as a minimum viable product designed to test critical assumptions, before committing to a solution fully?

descriptors.text: Has little or no practical knowledge of what makes a test or prototype useful.
Understands that testing an idea before committing fully reduces risk, without yet knowing what makes a test well designed.
Understands what makes a test or prototype useful, including testing critical assumptions before committing to a solution.
Has detailed understanding of designing tests that isolate and check critical assumptions; helps colleagues in their area of work design better tests.
Holds authoritative knowledge of test and prototype design; shapes standards or practice for how testing is done more widely.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in trying out new ideas on a small scale first — learning from what happens before committing to them fully?

descriptors.text: Has no experience of testing or prototyping ideas. Begins to understand why trying a small version of something before committing to it fully makes sense, and is curious about how this works in practice.

Participates in testing and prototyping activities when asked — such as giving feedback on a draft process, trying out a new approach and reporting what happened, or helping gather observations during a pilot. Understands that the purpose is to learn quickly rather than to produce something finished, and begins to think about what would need to be true for a test to be useful.

Applies straightforward methods to design and run simple experiments and build basic prototypes. Defines what the test needs to find out, chooses an approach that generates useful learning without over-investing in something unproven, and interprets evidence from the test to decide whether to refine, pivot or stop.

Designs and leads testing and prototyping activities that generate reliable learning efficiently. Selects appropriate methods based on what needs to be learned and the resources available, and ensures tests are designed to surface genuine insight rather than confirm existing assumptions. Helps colleagues develop more rigorous and imaginative approaches to testing and iteration.

Sets standards for how testing and prototyping are conducted across teams, ensuring experiments are well designed, ethically sound and genuinely iterative rather than performative. Builds team capability in lean experimentation and helps leaders understand how to create the governance and approval conditions that make rapid, low-cost testing possible in a public sector context.

rows.question: How would you rate how consistently you reflect on what worked and what didn't when you try something new or test an idea — and share what you found with others who might benefit?

descriptors.text: Has little habit of reflecting on what worked or didn't when trying something new. Begins to notice when an approach hasn't worked as expected and asks questions about what could be done differently next time.

Reflects on the outcomes of tests or new approaches they have participated in — noting what worked, what didn't and what they would do differently. Shares observations with immediate colleagues and recognises that what they learned could be useful to others facing similar challenges.

Systematically uses what they learn from testing to shape next steps — adjusting their approach, feeding findings back into a process or proposal, and deciding whether to refine, try something different or stop. Shares learning with colleagues in a way that is accessible and useful, rather than just reporting what happened.

Ensures that learning from testing is captured, shared and actively used to inform decisions across projects. Creates simple structures for reflecting on and documenting what was learned, and helps colleagues develop the habit of treating every test — successful or not — as a source of useful insight. Challenges the tendency to move on without extracting the full learning value from an experiment.

Builds team culture and processes that ensure learning from testing travels — across projects, teams and organisational boundaries — rather than staying with the individuals who ran the test. Establishes norms for knowledge sharing and reflection that make iterative learning a sustained organisational capability rather than a one-off activity.

skills.strand_definition: Communicates ideas for change in a way that genuinely persuades different audiences, framing evidence and impact so that decision-makers, colleagues and users understand why it matters.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of how to communicate an idea for change in a way that genuinely persuades different audiences?

descriptors.text: Has little formal knowledge of how to communicate ideas for change. Begins to notice that some people are more persuasive than others and is curious about what makes the difference.

Understands that communicating an idea for change requires more than explaining it clearly — it requires connecting it to what the audience cares about and addressing their concerns. Recognises that different audiences need to hear things differently and that evidence alone rarely persuades.

Understands the principles behind effective change communication — including how to structure a compelling narrative, how to connect an idea to outcomes that matter to different audiences, and why emotional resonance alongside evidence is important for building genuine support rather than passive compliance.

Has detailed knowledge of change communication theory and practice — including how to tailor messages for different stakeholders, how to anticipate and address resistance, and how to sustain engagement over the course of a change initiative rather than just at the point of launch.

Holds authoritative understanding of what makes change narratives work at an organisational level — including the research on persuasion, motivation and behaviour change that underpins effective advocacy. Uses this knowledge to advise others on communication strategy and to build organisational capability in change communication.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in tailoring your communication of ideas for change to different audiences, framing them in ways that connect to outcomes people genuinely care about?

descriptors.text: Has little experience of communicating ideas for change to different audiences. Begins to notice that the same explanation doesn't always land the same way with different people, and asks questions about how to frame ideas more effectively.

Explains ideas for improvement simply and clearly with guidance, adjusting basic language and emphasis for different audiences. Begins to think about what different audiences care about and tries to connect the idea to outcomes that are relevant to them, seeking feedback on whether the message has landed.

Adapts how they communicate ideas for change depending on the audience — adjusting language, emphasis and framing to connect the proposal to outcomes that matter to that audience. Structures explanations as a coherent narrative rather than a list of features, making clear what will change, why it matters and what it means for the people involved.

Constructs compelling narratives around proposed changes that resonate with varied audiences — from frontline colleagues to senior leaders — connecting the idea clearly to outcomes they genuinely value. Anticipates concerns and addresses them within the narrative rather than as afterthoughts, and helps colleagues develop their own ability to communicate change persuasively.

Sets standards for how change narratives are constructed and communicated across teams, ensuring they are consistently honest, audience-appropriate and connected to outcomes that matter. Builds team capability in persuasive change communication and models the kind of narrative craft that generates genuine understanding and lasting commitment rather than superficial agreement.

skills.strand_definition: Treats improvement as an ongoing habit, regularly reviewing how work is done and making evidence-based changes to processes, services and outcomes.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of structured approaches to continuous improvement — the principles, methods and tools that help teams regularly review and improve how they work?

descriptors.text: Has no formal knowledge of continuous improvement approaches. Begins to notice when processes feel unnecessarily slow or wasteful and is curious about whether there are structured ways to make them better.

Understands that continuous improvement means regularly reviewing how work is done and making evidence-based adjustments — rather than waiting for things to go wrong before changing them. Recognises that small, frequent improvements often deliver more lasting value than large one-off changes.

Understands the principles behind structured improvement approaches — including how to identify waste and inefficiency, how to use data and feedback to diagnose problems, and how to implement and monitor changes in a systematic way. Familiar with common improvement frameworks used in the public sector and can apply their underlying logic to everyday work.

Has detailed knowledge of continuous improvement methodologies — such as Lean, Plan-Do-Study-Act and Kaizen — and understands their relative strengths and limitations in a public sector context. Can advise colleagues on which approaches suit different types of problems and how to adapt improvement methods to work within organisational constraints.

Holds authoritative understanding of continuous improvement theory and practice — including how improvement methodologies connect to broader organisational learning, culture change and service transformation. Advises on how to build lasting improvement capability across teams and helps leaders understand the systemic conditions that enable or undermine continuous improvement at scale.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in implementing improvements deliberately and measuring whether they have had the effect you intended — rather than making changes and hoping for the best?

descriptors.text: Has little experience of implementing changes deliberately or checking whether they have worked. Begins to notice that changes sometimes don't have the effect people expected, and asks questions about how to tell whether something has actually improved.

Makes simple changes to how they work with guidance, and checks informally whether they have made a difference — such as asking colleagues whether a new approach feels better or tracking whether a recurring problem has reduced. Recognises that checking the impact of a change is as important as making it.

Implements changes in a planned way — defining what success looks like before making the change, monitoring what happens afterwards and adjusting if the change hasn't had the intended effect. Distinguishes between changes that have genuinely improved outcomes and those that have simply changed how work feels without making a measurable difference.

Leads improvement implementation across projects — ensuring changes are well planned, impact is measured rigorously and findings are used to refine further. Challenges changes that haven't been properly evaluated and helps colleagues develop more disciplined approaches to implementing and measuring improvement.

Sets standards for how improvements are implemented and evaluated across teams — ensuring that impact measurement is built into how change is managed rather than treated as an afterthought. Builds team capability in evidence-driven improvement and helps leaders understand the difference between activity and genuine, measurable progress.

rows.question: How would you rate how consistently you treat improvement as an ongoing habit — regularly reviewing how work is going and keeping that focus alive in your team even when other pressures mount?

descriptors.text: Has no established habit of regularly reviewing how work is going. Begins to notice when the same problems keep recurring and is curious about how teams maintain a focus on improvement over time rather than just fixing things when they break.

Regularly reflects on how their own work is going — noticing what's working well, what keeps going wrong and what small changes might help. Shares observations with colleagues and encourages others to do the same, recognising that improvement works best when it is a shared habit rather than an individual activity.

Consistently makes time to review how work is going — individually and with colleagues — and treats improvement as a regular part of how they work rather than an occasional project. Keeps momentum going by celebrating small improvements, acknowledging what has been learned from changes that didn't work, and encouraging colleagues to keep looking for ways to do things better.

Actively builds a team environment where continuous improvement is a shared expectation rather than an individual initiative — creating regular spaces for reflection, making it easy for colleagues to flag problems and suggest changes, and ensuring that improvement doesn't lose momentum when immediate pressures mount.

Embeds continuous improvement as a sustained cultural feature across teams — ensuring it is built into how work is planned, reviewed and celebrated rather than dependent on individual champions. Helps leaders understand the conditions that sustain an improvement culture over time and the signals that indicate it is starting to erode.

skills.strand_definition: Supports the adoption and spread of new approaches beyond a pilot or team, sustaining commitment and adapting what worked locally so it works more widely.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of what makes it hard to spread a successful idea or new way of working more widely — and what helps overcome those challenges?

descriptors.text: Has no formal knowledge of what scaling an innovation involves. Begins to notice that things which work well in one team or context don't always work the same way elsewhere, and is curious about why that happens.

Understands that scaling an innovation is harder than it might appear — that what works in a pilot doesn't automatically transfer to a wider context, and that successful adoption requires planning, communication and sustained support rather than simply rolling something out. Recognises that people's readiness and capacity to adopt change varies and that this affects how scaling needs to be managed.

Understands the key factors that determine whether an innovation scales successfully — including the importance of stakeholder buy-in, clear communication, adequate resource and support, and the need to adapt an approach for different contexts rather than assuming a one-size-fits-all rollout will work. Familiar with why innovations often stall between pilot and full adoption and what can be done to address this.

Has detailed knowledge of how to plan and manage the scaling of innovations in complex organisations — including implementation science principles, how to sequence adoption across different teams or contexts, and how to identify and address the organisational, cultural and practical barriers that prevent successful scaling. Can advise colleagues on what good scaling looks like and what the common failure points are.

Holds authoritative understanding of what makes innovation travel successfully across complex public sector organisations — including the systemic conditions, leadership behaviours and governance arrangements that enable or undermine scaling. Draws on theory and evidence to advise on scaling strategy and helps leaders understand why innovations that work at pilot stage so often fail to achieve lasting widespread adoption.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in actively supporting the adoption of new approaches — at whatever level your role allows, from helping a colleague understand a change to planning how it reaches different teams?

descriptors.text: Has no experience of helping spread a new approach beyond their immediate work. Begins to notice when colleagues are finding a change difficult to adopt and asks questions about what support would help them.

Supports the adoption of new approaches in their immediate context — helping colleagues understand what is changing and why, flagging where something isn't landing well and passing feedback to those leading the rollout. Recognises that successful adoption requires ongoing support rather than a single communication or training event.

Contributes actively to scaling efforts — adapting how a new approach is explained or implemented for different audiences and contexts, identifying where barriers to adoption are emerging and suggesting practical ways to address them. Keeps those leading the rollout informed of what is and isn't working on the ground.

Plans and manages the adoption of new approaches across teams or services — sequencing rollout thoughtfully, anticipating resistance and capacity constraints, and designing support that helps people genuinely embed a change rather than just comply with it. Addresses barriers proactively and adjusts the approach when adoption isn't progressing as intended.

Sets standards for how innovation is scaled across teams — ensuring rollout is planned, supported and evaluated in a way that leads to genuine embedding rather than superficial compliance. Builds organisational capability in managing adoption and helps leaders understand the human and cultural dimensions of scaling that determine whether an innovation sticks or fades.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in supporting and championing change to help maintain momentum — even when the initial excitement fades?

descriptors.text: Has little experience of sustaining commitment to a change over time. Begins to notice when enthusiasm for a new approach fades and people drift back to old habits, and is curious about what keeps some changes alive while others don't stick.

Continues to use and advocate for new approaches even when initial enthusiasm has faded and it would be easier to revert to old habits. Recognises that their own visible commitment to a change — however junior their role — signals to colleagues that it is worth persisting with.

Actively keeps momentum alive around changes they are involved in — checking in with colleagues on how adoption is going, acknowledging difficulties honestly, celebrating small wins and continuing to make the case for why the change matters even when other pressures make it tempting to let it slide.

Anticipates the point at which energy around a change typically fades and takes deliberate steps to sustain commitment — refreshing communication, reconnecting people to the reasons for the change, addressing emerging fatigue and ensuring that early adopters feel supported and recognised. Helps colleagues understand that the difficult middle period of a change is normal and manageable.

Builds organisational conditions that sustain commitment to change over the long term — ensuring that new approaches are embedded in processes, incentives and expectations rather than dependent on individual enthusiasm. Helps leaders understand the dynamics of change fatigue and the signals that indicate a change is starting to erode, and intervenes early to prevent drift back to old habits.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in actively connecting with colleagues in other teams, departments or organisations — sharing what has worked and helping proven approaches reach people who could benefit from them?

descriptors.text: Has little experience of building relationships beyond their immediate team. Begins to notice that good ideas often spread through personal connections rather than formal processes, and is open to sharing what they have learned with colleagues in other teams when the opportunity arises.

Shares what their team has tried and learned with colleagues outside their immediate context, and is receptive to hearing what others are doing differently. Recognises that building relationships across organisational boundaries makes it easier for successful approaches to spread, and looks for informal opportunities to make those connections.

Actively builds relationships with colleagues in other teams and organisations who are working on similar challenges — sharing what has worked, learning from their experience and making connections that help proven approaches travel beyond their original context. Represents their team's work externally and helps others understand what they have learned and how it might apply elsewhere.

Deliberately cultivates partnerships across organisational boundaries that enable successful innovations to spread — identifying who needs to know about a proven approach, brokering connections between teams with relevant experience and ensuring that knowledge about what works doesn't stay siloed. Builds relationships with external organisations, other government departments and professional networks that keep their team connected to the wider innovation landscape.

Builds and sustains cross-organisational partnerships and networks that systematically enable innovation to travel across government — ensuring that proven approaches reach the teams and contexts where they could deliver the greatest value. Establishes lasting relationships with external partners, other departments and international peers that create ongoing channels for shared learning and collaborative innovation at scale.

domains.domain_description: Using and governing artificial intelligence responsibly — including machine learning, automation, classification, recommendation and generative AI. This domain is here as AI appears in everyday tools and in higher-stakes services. Most colleagues need foundational literacy and sound judgement about outputs. Governance and ethics matter more when you use, commission or influence AI systems.

skills.strand_definition: Builds foundational understanding of what AI is, how it works and what it can and cannot do across machine learning, automation and generative AI, and develops the practical skills needed to specify inputs, use tools effectively and work critically with outputs in everyday work.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of what AI is, how it works and what it can and cannot do?

descriptors.text: Basic or minimal knowledge; knows that AI tools exist and are used in government but has little understanding of how they work or what they can do.

Understands what common AI tools do and broadly how they work; knows that AI outputs depend on inputs such as training data and that different AI approaches (e.g. prediction, classification, generative text) suit different tasks.

Confidently understands how different AI types generate outputs, what their limitations are, and what failure modes mean for how outputs should be used — including hallucination and bias for generative systems, and false positives/negatives, drift and overfitting for prediction and classification systems.

Deep understanding of AI capabilities and limitations across different types including generative AI, predictive models, classification, recommendation and automation; advises colleagues on appropriate use and potential harms.
Authoritative knowledge of the AI landscape; shapes how AI is understood and used responsibly across teams and stays current with developments in AI capabilities and risks.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in using AI tools in your everyday work?

descriptors.text: Uses AI tools with direct support; needs guidance on which tools are appropriate and how to use them for basic tasks.
Uses familiar AI tools independently for simple, everyday tasks; knows which approved tools are available and follows organisational guidance on their use.
Uses a range of AI tools confidently and independently in own work; selects the right tool for the task and applies AI where it genuinely adds value.
Uses AI tools fluently across varied contexts; helps colleagues identify and adopt tools that improve their work and shares practical knowledge of effective use.
Sets the standard for effective AI tool use across teams; ensures colleagues have the skills and confidence to use AI tools well and stays current with new tools and capabilities.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in specifying and preparing inputs so AI systems produce reliable, useful outputs?

descriptors.text: Follows basic guidance on inputs — such as example prompts or provided reference data — with support; needs help understanding why inputs affect output quality.
Prepares simple inputs independently — for example clear prompts with purpose and audience, or appropriate reference data — and understands that input quality shapes results.

Specifies effective inputs for a range of everyday AI uses; for generative tools, frames prompts neutrally and iterates when outputs miss the mark; for other systems, recognises when training data, thresholds or context need checking; confirms outputs address the task before use.

Develops and shares effective input practices across AI types and contexts; coaches colleagues on clear specification and neutral framing where bias could be introduced; troubleshoots poor outputs by revisiting inputs and configuration.

Sets standards for how teams specify and validate inputs across AI systems; stays current with evolving practice; ensures colleagues understand how leading inputs or poor reference data can compromise high-stakes work such as policy advice.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in checking whether an AI output is reliable before acting on it or sharing it with others?

descriptors.text: Beginning to notice that AI outputs might not always be right; tends to accept what AI produces without applying own judgment.
Recognises that AI outputs can be wrong or misleading; approaches them with some caution and seeks guidance before acting on outputs that seem uncertain.
Consistently approaches AI outputs critically; questions what AI produces, considers limitations and does not use outputs without applying own judgment.
Models critical engagement with AI outputs; challenges colleagues who accept AI outputs uncritically and promotes a questioning approach across the team.
Champions a culture of critical AI literacy across teams; ensures that questioning AI outputs is treated as standard practice rather than optional, especially in high-stakes decisions.

skills.strand_definition: Identifies where AI and automation could add genuine value, and recognises the limitations and risks that could make AI unsuitable.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of where AI and automation can and cannot add value — including what kinds of tasks AI tends to help with and what makes some tasks unsuitable?

descriptors.text: Basic or minimal knowledge; knows that AI can improve some processes but has little understanding of where it adds value or why it might not be suitable.
Understands the types of tasks and processes where AI is most likely to add value; knows that suitability depends on factors like data quality, process stability and the nature of the task.

Confidently understands where AI and automation can and cannot add value across a range of task types; knows what makes a task well-suited to AI and what constraints — technical, ethical or practical — might make it unsuitable.

Deep understanding of the conditions under which AI delivers genuine value; advises on where AI investment is likely to be worthwhile and where it is not, drawing on evidence and experience across different contexts.
Authoritative knowledge of AI opportunity and constraint across the full range of AI types; shapes how AI potential is assessed across teams and ensures adoption is evidence-based and proportionate.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in identifying tasks, inefficiencies or pain points that AI could help address?

descriptors.text: Begins to notice that some tasks might benefit from AI; tends toward an all-or-nothing view of what AI can do rather than seeing specific opportunities clearly.
Identifies simple opportunities where AI could reduce repetitive work or improve efficiency; shares ideas with colleagues and is open to exploring what might be possible.
Actively identifies tasks, inefficiencies and pain points in own work and service processes where AI could add genuine value; develops initial ideas and engages others to test assumptions.

Leads structured identification of AI opportunities across a team or area of work; uses evidence and insight to pinpoint where AI could have the highest impact and builds a credible case for investment.
Shapes how AI opportunities are identified across teams; builds the culture, networks and frameworks needed to surface transformative ideas and turn them into lasting improvements.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in weighing up whether AI is the right solution for a problem, taking into account its limitations and risks alongside its potential benefits?

descriptors.text: Aware that AI has some limitations but may not yet understand what they are; tends to either dismiss AI entirely or accept it uncritically rather than identifying specific risks or constraints.
Recognises common constraints that affect AI suitability such as poor data quality, unstable processes or regulatory requirements; follows guidance to weigh these against potential benefits.

Confidently identifies limitations and risks that could make AI unsuitable for a given task — including data gaps, ethical concerns, high-stakes decisions and tasks requiring human judgment; uses this to make well-rounded recommendations.

Anticipates complex constraints including ethical implications, change impact and long-term risk; helps colleagues recognise limitations they may have missed and ensures proposals are realistic and responsible.

Ensures AI is only adopted where limitations have been thoroughly assessed and mitigated; shapes how risk and constraint evaluation is done across teams and aligns adoption with strategy, ethics and regulation.

skills.strand_definition: Uses AI tools and automation safely in everyday work — knowing which tools are approved, what data can be shared with them, spotting when a prompt or task carries risk, and escalating when something feels wrong.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of your organisation's rules on which AI tools are approved for use and what data can safely be shared with them?

descriptors.text: Has little or no practical knowledge of which AI tools are approved or what data can safely be shared with them.
Understands that rules exist on approved tools and data sharing, and knows where to find them.
Understands which tools are approved for their own work and what data can and cannot be shared with them.
Has detailed understanding of the reasoning behind approval and data-sharing rules; explains them to colleagues and flags situations the guidance does not clearly cover.
Holds authoritative knowledge of approval and data-handling rules across tools and contexts; shapes or advises on the policy itself.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in spotting when a specific AI prompt or task carries a safety risk — whether from the data it contains or from the nature of the task itself — and adjusting or stopping before proceeding?

descriptors.text: Cannot yet reliably spot when a prompt or task carries a safety risk without direct support; with support, begins to avoid obviously sensitive data in prompts.
Uses basic checks with support to recognise common data risks in prompts; relies on others to judge whether a task itself is appropriate.
Applies safety checks independently in routine situations, spotting both data exposure and tasks unsuited to AI, and adjusts or stops accordingly.
Uses judgement independently across varied scenarios to spot subtler risks that are not obviously about data; helps colleagues in their area of work see them too.
Leads application of safety judgement across teams or services in novel or ambiguous situations; shapes guidance or standards others rely on.

rows.question: How would you rate your ability to escalate concerns about AI use to the right person when something feels wrong?

descriptors.text: Shows curiosity and asks questions when something feels wrong, but needs prompting to know what to do about it.
Raises concerns with a manager or colleague when encouraged, with support when needed; may hesitate to act alone without support.
Escalates concerns about AI use consistently in everyday work, promptly and without needing to be prompted.
Coaches and supports others informally by spotting subtle or complex risks and escalating with enough detail for action to be taken.
Shapes standards by exercising authoritative judgement on when AI use crosses a line, including risks existing guidance does not yet cover.

skills.strand_definition: Develops the skills and behaviours needed to check, interpret and communicate AI outputs critically and honestly — maintaining human judgment and transparency rather than deferring uncritically to AI recommendations.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of how AI generates outputs and why they may be unreliable or biased?

descriptors.text: Basic or minimal knowledge; knows that AI outputs can be wrong but may not understand why.

Understands that AI outputs can be inaccurate, uncertain or biased; knows that outputs are shaped by the data the system was trained on and that checking them is important for fair and transparent decisions.

Confidently understands why AI outputs may be unreliable — including hallucination, bias from training data, overconfidence and lack of context; knows how to recognise these issues and what they mean for how outputs should be used.

Deep understanding of how different AI types generate outputs, their specific failure modes and how patterns of error or bias can be identified and documented; the person others turn to when AI outputs need scrutinising.
Authoritative knowledge of AI output reliability, evaluation methods and documentation standards; shapes how outputs are reviewed, challenged and explained across teams and in high-stakes decisions.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in checking and interpreting AI outputs before acting on them?

descriptors.text: Checks AI outputs with direct support; needs guidance to understand what an output means and whether it can be trusted.
Applies basic checks to AI outputs with light support; asks questions about how results were generated and avoids acting on them without verifying.
Checks and interprets AI outputs independently; compares them with other evidence, looks for errors or bias and applies consistent checks before acting.
Tests AI outputs rigorously across varied scenarios; identifies patterns of error or bias, suggests improvements and reviews colleagues interpretations for accuracy.
Sets standards for how AI outputs are checked and documented across teams; guides high-stakes decisions and ensures review processes are robust and consistently applied.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in making clear to others when a decision or recommendation has been informed by AI — including what that means for how certain you are?

descriptors.text: Beginning to notice that AI involvement in a decision or output is worth mentioning; does not yet do this consistently or know how to explain uncertainty.
Acknowledges when AI has contributed to a decision or recommendation and flags basic limitations to colleagues in plain terms.
Consistently transparent about AIs role in decisions and recommendations; clearly communicates uncertainty and limitations so others can make informed judgments.
Actively ensures AI contributions and their limitations are clearly communicated in all relevant contexts; challenges colleagues who present AI outputs without appropriate caveats.
Champions transparency about AI use and uncertainty across teams; sets standards for how AI contributions are disclosed and documented, including in high-stakes decisions.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in deciding when to trust an AI output and when to question or override it?

descriptors.text: Beginning to notice that AI outputs might not always be right; tends to accept what AI produces without applying own judgment.
Recognises the importance of human judgment alongside AI; avoids accepting recommendations blindly and asks questions before acting on outputs.
Consistently exercises own judgment when working with AI outputs; treats AI as one input among several rather than the final word, and overrides it when evidence or experience suggests otherwise.
Actively guards against automation bias in own and others work; coaches colleagues to apply independent judgment and challenges decisions that defer uncritically to AI.
Leads a culture of human oversight across teams; ensures AI is used as a tool to support judgment rather than replace it, particularly in high-stakes decisions affecting citizens.

skills.strand_definition: Understands and applies the legal, regulatory and compliance frameworks that govern AI use in public services — including identifying and responding to governance risks.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of the legal and regulatory frameworks that govern AI use?

descriptors.text: Basic or minimal knowledge; knows that AI use is governed by rules and policies but has little understanding of what they are.
Understands the key legal and regulatory requirements that apply to AI use; knows where to find guidance and who to ask when unsure.

Confidently understands how relevant laws, regulations and organisational policies apply to AI use in own context; knows how governance frameworks connect to accountability and compliance, and recognises that rules are a minimum standard rather than the whole picture.
Deep understanding of AI governance frameworks, regulatory requirements and accountability structures; recognises when compliance alone is not enough and knows when to look beyond the rules.

Authoritative knowledge of AI law, regulation and governance; identifies gaps where existing frameworks have not kept pace with technology, advocates for stronger governance and shapes how frameworks are understood and applied across teams.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in applying governance and compliance requirements when using or commissioning AI?

descriptors.text: Follows agreed rules and policies when using AI tools with direct support; asks for help when unsure whether something is permitted.
Applies basic governance requirements reliably with light support; checks that AI use follows organisational policy and knows who to contact when requirements are unclear.
Applies relevant governance and compliance requirements confidently in everyday AI use; ensures AI tools and outputs meet organisational and regulatory standards before acting on them.
Leads compliance across a team or area of work; ensures AI use meets all relevant legal and regulatory requirements and coaches colleagues on their governance obligations.
Sets governance standards for AI use across teams; ensures compliance frameworks are practical, up to date and consistently applied.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in identifying and responding to governance and compliance risks in AI use?

descriptors.text: Recognises that some AI use may carry risks; flags concerns with a manager or appropriate contact with direct support.
Identifies obvious governance risks such as using unapproved tools or sharing data inappropriately; escalates promptly and follows guidance on how to respond.
Identifies and responds to governance risks in own AI use; applies agreed processes to mitigate risks and reports issues before they escalate.
Reviews AI use across a team or area of work for governance risks; leads responses to compliance issues and strengthens processes to prevent recurrence.
Shapes how governance risks are identified and managed across teams; ensures risk management processes are robust, proportionate and consistently applied.

skills.strand_definition: Applies ethical principles to AI use in public services — including fairness, transparency to citizens, public benefit and consideration of wider societal and environmental impact — grounded in the Data and AI Ethics Framework and UK AI regulatory principles.

rows.question: How would you rate your understanding of the ethical principles that should guide responsible AI use in public services?

descriptors.text: Has little knowledge of the ethical principles that apply to AI in public services, but begins to notice situations where AI use might raise concerns about fairness, transparency or harm — including environmental cost.

Understands the key ethical principles that apply to AI — including fairness, transparency, avoiding harm to people and minimising environmental impact — and can recognise when they are relevant in simple situations.

Applies ethical principles confidently in everyday AI use. Understands how fairness, transparency, wider societal impact and environmental sustainability apply to the AI tools and approaches used in own work.

Applies detailed knowledge of ethical principles across a team or area of work; ensures AI use reflects fairness, transparency, accountability and environmental responsibility, and stays current with evolving guidance and legislation.

Authoritative knowledge of ethical principles for AI in public services; shapes how they are understood and applied across teams, advocates for stronger standards where needed, and stays current with evolving guidance and legislation — including emerging requirements on environmental sustainability.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in applying fairness and public benefit considerations when using or recommending AI?

descriptors.text: Recognises that AI can produce unfair or biased outcomes but needs support to identify when this is happening or what to do about it.
Considers whether AI use is fair and likely to be beneficial; flags concerns when something seems discriminatory, harmful or contrary to the public interest, with guidance on how to respond.
Applies fairness and public benefit considerations to own AI use; identifies when AI may produce inequitable outcomes for different groups and raises this appropriately before decisions are made.

Leads fairness and public benefit assessments across a team or area of work; ensures AI use actively serves the public interest, addresses bias and considers impact on different groups including those who may be disadvantaged.

Shapes how fairness and public benefit are assessed and embedded across teams; ensures AI adoption is genuinely equitable, challenges use that fails to meet this standard, and advocates for those most at risk of harm.

rows.question: How would you rate your competence in making AI use transparent and explainable to those affected by it?

descriptors.text: Recognises that people affected by AI decisions have a right to understand how those decisions were made; needs support to explain AI use to others in practice.
Understands why transparency with affected people matters; can explain AI use in simple, honest terms with light guidance and knows when to seek help for more complex situations.

Ensures people affected by AI-informed decisions in own work understand how AI was used and what it contributed; recognises that transparency about process and outcomes can and should be provided even where the technical detail of an AI system cannot be disclosed.

Ensures transparency and explainability are built into how AI is used and communicated across a team; helps colleagues explain AI use clearly to those affected, ensures people know how to raise concerns or challenge decisions, and understands which types of transparency are appropriate in which circumstances — including when technical transparency is not possible.

Sets standards for transparency and explainability in AI use across teams; ensures those affected by AI decisions can understand, question and challenge them through genuinely accessible routes, including in situations where full technical transparency is not possible for security or operational reasons — ensuring process and outcome transparency fill that gap.

rows.question: How would you rate your ability to consider the wider and longer-term effects of using AI — including on people who won't be in the room when decisions are made?

descriptors.text: Beginning to notice that AI can affect people beyond those directly involved; does not yet consider this consistently or know how to act on it.
Considers the wider impact of AI use on people and communities, including those who may not have a say in how AI is used; raises concerns when impacts seem harmful or disproportionate.

Consistently considers the wider and longer-term impact of AI in own work — including on people who are affected but have no voice in the decision — and raises this proactively rather than waiting to be asked.

Actively ensures the impact of AI on people with no direct voice is considered across a team or area of work; builds this into how decisions are made, ensures environmental and societal consequences are part of the conversation, and challenges decisions that overlook these impacts.

Champions consideration of wider societal and environmental impact in AI use across teams; creates the conditions for those with no voice to be represented in decision-making, takes long-term consequences seriously and holds the organisation accountable for the broader effects of its AI use.

rows.question: How would you rate your ability to factor in the environmental cost of AI when deciding whether and how to use it?
rows.source_note: Grounded in GDS Design Principle 11 (environmental sustainability, added April 2025) and the GDS Data and AI Ethics Framework sustainability principle. Flagged amber — inferred application of official principles to civil servant behaviour.

descriptors.text: Not yet aware that AI tools have an environmental cost. Begins to notice when this is mentioned and asks questions about what it means in practice.
Understands that AI tools use significant energy and that choosing them proportionately is part of responsible use. Begins to consider whether AI is the right tool for a task before using it.

Consistently considers whether AI is the most proportionate tool for a task — for example, using a search engine rather than a generative AI tool for a simple factual query. Avoids unnecessary or repeated AI use when simpler alternatives work just as well.

Actively promotes proportionate AI use across a team or area of work. Reviews how AI tools are used, identifies patterns of unnecessary or wasteful use, and coaches colleagues to make more sustainable choices. Flags environmental considerations when AI adoption decisions are being made.

Embeds environmental sustainability into team expectations and standards for AI use. Ensures that guidance, training and procurement processes reflect the principle that AI should be used proportionately and that its resource costs are a legitimate factor in adoption decisions. Connects this to broader organisational commitments on sustainability.

innovation_question_design_principles.title: Question design principles for the DDI & AI Skills and Capabilities Framework

principles.title: Questions must work without the descriptors
principles.detail: The intended delivery model may involve a condensed question visible to the user with descriptors sitting in the background, accessed by an LLM in a conversational self-assessment interface. Questions must be self-evidently clear without any scaffolding.

principles.title: Avoid jargon and specialist vocabulary
principles.detail: Questions should be answerable by someone who has never encountered the technical term behind the row. 'Psychological safety' becomes 'what makes people feel safe to suggest new ideas.' 'Prototyping' becomes 'trying something out on a small scale.' The LLM can introduce technical vocabulary naturally in conversation once the person has engaged with the concept.

principles.title: K, S and B rows need different question framings
principles.detail: K rows should use 'how well do you understand...' S rows should describe a specific action or technique — 'do you...' anchored to what someone does rather than what they know. B rows should describe a consistent habit or disposition — 'do you...' framed as frequency or regularity, not methodology. Watch for 'how' at the start of B row questions, which can accidentally read as 'by what method' rather than 'to what degree.'

principles.title: Avoid assessing confidence rather than the behaviour itself
principles.detail: Questions like 'how confidently do you...' assess confidence rather than the skill or behaviour. Reframe as 'do you...' or 'how well do you...' depending on row type.

principles.title: Avoid questions that assess context rather than the person
principles.detail: Some questions inadvertently assess the person's environment rather than their own skill. Questions should be anchored to what the person knows, does and values, not whether their environment makes it easy or hard.

principles.title: The training mapping test
principles.detail: For every row, ask: what course would teach this? If you can't identify a coherent course, the row may be a behaviour or disposition rather than a teachable skill — and may belong in a B row rather than an S row, or may not warrant a standalone row at all.

principles.title: Questions should be accessible to non-specialists at all grades
principles.detail: For rows where the full skill is only realistic at higher grades, the question should still be answerable by someone at Novice or Awareness level — describing the participatory or observational version of the behaviour. 'At whatever level your role allows' is a useful phrase for rows that span a wide range of roles and grades.

principles.title: Avoid questions that assume a positive or change-friendly environment
principles.detail: Questions shouldn't assume the person is enthusiastic about a change, that their organisation is supportive, or that things are going well. Neutral phrasing holds the possibility that honest assessment might mean flagging problems rather than advocating.

principles.title: When in doubt, give people more to hook into
principles.detail: Abstract questions leave people without enough to orient themselves. Adding a concrete clause gives people an immediate reference point without making the question unwieldy.

principles.title: The 'both halves' instinct
principles.detail: Several of the best questions emerged from combining elements of two options rather than choosing one wholesale. When two options each capture something the other misses, look for a formulation that holds both — usually by taking the situating clause from one and the behaviour description from the other.
